title: Unit Circle Basics Quiz
intro: Answer these questions to check your understanding of the unit circle, where angles in radians equal arc lengths, x and y coordinates are cosine and sine, and the running example uses arc length 1.047 reaching the point (0.500, 0.866).

questions.prompt: On the unit circle, is every point exactly distance 1 from the origin?
questions.explanation: The unit circle is defined as the set of all points exactly 1 unit from the center, so the white circle outline confirms that every radius segment measures 1.
questions.hint: Recall the definition shown by the ruler on the white circle.
questions.why_it_matters: This confirms the learner accepts the basic geometric definition before assigning coordinates.

questions.prompt: If the orange arc on the unit circle measures 1.047, what is the angle θ in radians? Round to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: By definition on the unit circle, the angle θ in radians is identical to the arc length of the orange arc, so the displayed length 1.047 is θ itself.
questions.hint: The orange arc length and the θ label are the same number.
questions.why_it_matters: This verifies the learner understands radians as arc length rather than an arbitrary unit.

questions.prompt: At the running-example arc length 1.047, is the point reached in the first quadrant?
questions.explanation: The orange arc of length 1.047 starts at (1,0) and travels counterclockwise less than a quarter turn, landing where both the blue x segment and green y segment are positive.
questions.hint: Think about where one-sixth of the way around the circle lands.
questions.why_it_matters: This checks that the learner can locate the point using the angle before naming the coordinates.

questions.prompt: At θ = 1.047, which length is labeled cosine and which is labeled sine?

choices.text: The blue horizontal length is cosine and the green vertical length is sine.
The green vertical length is cosine and the blue horizontal length is sine.
Both lengths together are called cosine.
Both lengths together are called sine.

questions.explanation: The blue segment measures the horizontal distance x and receives the label cos θ; the green segment measures the vertical distance y and receives the label sin θ.
questions.hint: Watch which color segment gets which label when the arc stops.
questions.why_it_matters: This ensures the learner connects the coordinate lengths directly to the names cosine and sine.

questions.prompt: Round to three decimal places: what is sin(1.047) for the running-example point?
questions.explanation: The green vertical segment at arc length 1.047 measures 0.866, and that length is defined as sin θ.
questions.hint: Look at the length of the green segment in the running example.
questions.why_it_matters: This confirms the learner can read the sine value directly from the coordinate on the unit circle.

questions.prompt: For the running-example point, is 0.500 squared plus 0.866 squared equal to 1.000?
questions.explanation: The blue and green segments form the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the radius 1, so Pythagoras requires their squares to sum exactly to 1.
questions.hint: Imagine the two square areas growing from the blue and green segments and compare their total to the radius square.
questions.why_it_matters: This shows the learner sees the Pythagorean identity as a visible geometric fact rather than a memorized rule.

questions.prompt: Round to three decimal places: what is cos(1.047) for the running-example point?
questions.explanation: The blue horizontal segment at arc length 1.047 measures 0.500, and that length is defined as cos θ.
questions.hint: Look at the length of the blue segment in the running example.
questions.why_it_matters: This confirms the learner can read the cosine value directly from the coordinate on the unit circle.

questions.prompt: Why must the square of the blue length plus the square of the green length always equal 1 at any angle on the unit circle?

choices.text: Because sine and cosine are defined that way on a calculator.
Because the blue and green segments form the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse equal to the radius 1.
Because the orange arc length forces the sum to be 1.
Because the x-axis and y-axis are perpendicular by definition.

questions.explanation: The blue horizontal and green vertical segments are the two legs of the right triangle whose hypotenuse is the fixed radius of length 1, so their squares sum to 1 by the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.hint: Focus on the right triangle formed by the two colored segments and the radius.
questions.why_it_matters: This verifies the learner can explain the identity geometrically using the running example rather than treating it as arbitrary.
